prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, founding moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the cleanest theory-to-experiment story on the shortlist. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model (2011) predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity by Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators confirmed that a simple carbon system with a tunable control parameter hosts strongly correlated phases. As someone working on many-body and stochastic problems, I value that a single geometric knob gives access to Mott-like and superconducting physics in one device, and that the phenomenology has been reproduced across many laboratories, platforms and measurement techniques. The theory and experiment map onto the three supplied names without strain, and the field it created (moire quantum materials) is already broad and still productive.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old, and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated states are unsettled, so a prize could be seen as slightly early and as honouring a prediction plus a first observation rather than a settled understanding. Experimental credit is also diffuse: the first-author student, hBN-encapsulated device work, and later groups (Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and others) are not in the credited names, so a three-person cap leaves real attribution costs. Opening support from three of us should not be mistaken for proof that the discovery is the strongest on the merits.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B022 first because the correlated phases were measured, not merely proposed, and the experiments are robust across laboratories, while noting that experimental credit is partly shared beyond the supplied names.
responses.response: I agree that the robustness of the measured phenomenology is the decisive point, and I share the worry about the experimental side. I would add that this is exactly why a theory-plus-experiment configuration is the fairer framing: Bistritzer and MacDonald made a specific, falsifiable prediction years before the measurement, and Jarillo-Herrero's group is the first to have shown the correlated and superconducting states. The collaborators outside the names are a limitation of the three-person rule, not a reason to downgrade the discovery.

responses.point: Johansson places B022 only sixth and calls recognition slightly premature, citing sample-to-sample variability and the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity.
responses.response: I take the maturity concern seriously, and it is my main reservation as well. But I think it conflates the discovery with its full explanation. The existence of flat bands near the magic angle, the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes are reproduced widely and are not in doubt; only the pairing mechanism is open. Prizes have regularly honoured a discovery before its microscopic theory was complete. I would be more persuaded by your caution if the reproducibility itself were in question, and I do not think it is.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clocks first: independent confirmation at 10^-18 across laboratories, a clean Katori-Ye attribution, and recognition that is timely and not premature.
responses.response: The clock case is strong on maturity and attribution, and I regard it as the best-defined two-person configuration we have; that is why I list it as an alternative. My disagreement is about the type of discovery. The lattice clock is an outstanding instrument and a precise measurement platform, whereas twisted bilayer graphene revealed a new regime of matter and generated a research field. If we apply the criterion of lasting benefit through new understanding, I weigh the latter more heavily, though not so heavily that I would oppose the clocks if the committee prefers a cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B012 first as a concrete invention with a clear discovery narrative, and ranks B022 second, noting that the experimental credit is shared with students and collaborators and that the line is not fully settled.
responses.response: I agree with you that the attribution line is not fully settled on the experimental side, and I would not claim it is. Where I differ is that a shared experimental credit is common for modern materials experiments and has not stopped us before; the prize can recognise the group leader while the citation names the discovery. I also accept your point that the transport, scanning-probe and device-assembly evidence is what makes the claim secure, and I would want the citation to say so rather than lean only on the theory prediction.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B022 first as an example of band-structure reasoning anticipating a new phase, but notes that other theory groups contributed to the flat-band physics and that credit for the first experiments involves a larger team.
responses.response: I agree that other theory groups worked on flat bands and moire structures, and I cannot settle that from the supplied names. What distinguishes the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is that it identified the magic angle quantitatively and in a form that experiments could target. That is the contribution that connects to the 2018 measurements, so I consider the supplied theory credit defensible. I would welcome any colleague's specific objection about priority, since I am a statistical physicist and not a band-structure specialist.

uncertainties: Whether the pairing mechanism and the correlated-state physics must be better understood before the discovery is considered mature enough.
Whether the experimental credit should centre on Jarillo-Herrero alone given the contributions of students, hBN-device work and other groups outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee prefers a theory-and-experiment prize on a young field over the cleaner, more mature clock configuration (B012).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: my documented co-authors and institutions (Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) do not include any of MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Katori, Ye, or the B056 candidates.
